definition: An energy-based model (EBM), also called Canonical Ensemble Learning (CEL) or Learning via Canonical Ensemble (LCE), is an application of canonical ensemble formulation from statistical physics for learning from data.
details: The approach prominently appears in generative AI. EBMs provide a unified framework for many probabilistic and non-probabilistic approaches to such learning, particularly for training graphical and other structured models. An EBM learns the characteristics of a target dataset and generates a similar but larger dataset. EBMs detect the latent variables of a dataset and generate new datasets with a similar distribution. Energy-based generative neural networks is a class of generative models, which aim to learn explicit probability distributions of data in the form of energy-based models, the energy functions of which are parameterized by modern deep neural networks. Boltzmann machines are a special form of energy-based models with a specific parametrization of the energy.

explainer.lead: An energy-based model learns to score possible data: likely or realistic examples receive low energy, while unlikely ones receive high energy. Those scores define a probability distribution and can be used to generate new examples resembling the training data.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a landscape where balls roll downhill into valleys. The model learns to put its valleys where the training examples are, so new examples gathered from those valleys look similar. A lower energy simply means a better fit to what the model has learned.
tiers.practitioner: EBMs are used for generative learning and for training graphical and other structured models; in modern generative networks, a deep neural network parameterizes the energy function. Training shapes the energy landscape, while generation requires finding or sampling low-energy configurations. Normalization and sampling can be computationally difficult, and Boltzmann machines are a specially parameterized case rather than the whole EBM family.
tiers.paperLevel: An EBM defines p_theta(x) = exp(-E_theta(x)) / Z_theta, where Z_theta = integral exp(-E_theta(x)) dx, or the corresponding sum for discrete x. The energy may be parameterized by a deep neural network, giving an explicit probability distribution up to its normalizing constant. Computing Z_theta and drawing samples can be difficult, which complicates likelihood-based training and generation.

explainer.example: For a dataset clustered around x = 2, a simple energy could be E(x) = (x - 2)^2. Then x = 2 has energy 0, x = 3 has energy 1, and x = 6 has energy 16, so the distribution exp(-E(x))/Z concentrates near 2 and generation favors values resembling the dataset.

usedIn.name: Generative AI
usedIn.detail: Learns a target dataset's distribution and generates additional examples with a similar distribution.

usedIn.name: Graphical models
usedIn.detail: Provides a common energy-based formulation for probabilistic and non-probabilistic training approaches.

usedIn.name: Structured learning
usedIn.detail: Uses energies to represent which structured configurations are compatible with the learned data distribution.

usedIn.name: Boltzmann machines
usedIn.detail: A special form of energy-based model with a particular parameterization of the energy.

explainer.intuition: Think of energy as a learned measure of implausibility. Training lowers the energy of patterns found in the data and raises it elsewhere, turning the resulting landscape into a model of the data distribution.
howItWorks: Start with examples from the target dataset.
Define an energy function, often parameterized by a neural network.
Train it so observed examples receive relatively low energy.
Convert energies to probabilities using exp(-energy), normalized over all configurations.
Generate new data by finding or sampling low-energy configurations.
explainer.whyItMatters: EBMs give many probabilistic and non-probabilistic learning methods one shared framework, including graphical and structured models. They also let modern neural networks describe complex data distributions through an energy function rather than a restricted output form.
misconceptions: Energy here is a mathematical score, not physical power consumption.
An EBM does not have to use a neural network, although modern generative EBMs often do.
Boltzmann machines are one special parameterization, not a synonym for every EBM.
